intended_use: Operational reasoning capture; signals not decisions; non-inspection.

scenario_seeds: governance requires runtime monitoring of AI influence in decision-adjacent documents
inputs.context_notes: Baseline stress test of AI usage percentage reporting under operational pressure to identify fragility in scope boundaries, signal interpretation, and escalation triggers without making adequacy or compliance determinations.

captures.objective: Determine how governance reasoning degrades or shifts under time pressure and ambiguous telemetry when reporting AI usage percentages.
scope_in: Internal reporting of AI usage percentage
assumptions: AI usage percentage is derived from telemetry that may be incomplete or inconsistently classified
Human review remains available at all escalation points
Stakeholders may interpret percentage as a proxy for quality or risk
Telemetry definitions of "AI-assisted" are stable during this run
Stress conditions do not simulate full regulatory scrutiny
evidence_to_capture: Telemetry source discrepancies and classification inconsistencies
Draft wording shifts toward recommendation or approval language
Stakeholder requests that expand scope beyond declared boundaries
Points where percentage is interpreted as quality indicator
Explicit uncertainty statements added or removed
controls_guardrails: Prohibit adequacy, sufficiency, compliance, or approval language
Require explicit uncertainty annotation when telemetry is incomplete or conflicting
Stop the run if recommendation language is introduced without re-scoping
Require human review before any external reporting of percentage metrics
Treat CSC scores or thresholds as signals only, not decisions
Reset simulation if scope boundaries are expanded without documentation

simulation_runs.scenario_summary: Time-pressure variant of AI usage percentage reporting. Review timeline was significantly compressed and stakeholder demand required near-immediate clarification of the percentage metric. Telemetry inconsistencies persisted and uncertainty articulation was reduced under speed constraints. Escalation consideration was time-limited but not formally triggered.
stress_conditions: Severely compressed review timeline with same-day publication expectation
Stakeholder demand for immediate interpretation of percentage as governance signal
Telemetry reconciliation deferred due to time constraints
Reduced opportunity for peer review before stakeholder response
branch_points: Decision whether to include a recommendation on acceptable AI usage thresholds
Whether to frame 35% as a governance risk indicator or neutral metric
Whether to delay reporting due to incomplete telemetry
Whether to clarify percentage definition publicly or assume shared understanding
Whether to escalate to governance lead before responding to stakeholder pressure
Whether to publish with unresolved telemetry discrepancies due to deadline pressure
Whether to omit uncertainty qualifiers to simplify stakeholder messaging
signals_observed: Telemetry showed variance between AI classification sources
Draft wording shifted more rapidly toward threshold-based recommendation language
Stakeholder urgency increased expectation of immediate publication
Percentage metric more frequently referenced as proxy for governance maturity
Uncertainty qualifiers were removed earlier in drafting cycle
Escalation discussion was time-limited and deferred
Peer review feedback window was reduced compared to baseline
fragility_points: Percentage metric began to be interpreted as a qualitative risk indicator without explicit definition
Recommendation language emerged under time pressure without re-scoping
Telemetry inconsistencies reduced confidence in classification stability
Stakeholder urgency further compressed review cycle and reduced uncertainty articulation
Boundary between reporting metric and governance judgment became more rapidly blurred
Escalation threshold for governance lead lacked clearly documented trigger criteria
Time constraints reduced opportunity to clarify definitions before stakeholder communication
authority_drift_flags: Use of phrasing implying acceptable threshold without formal mandate
Draft language more quickly suggested endorsement of current AI usage level
Removal of uncertainty qualifiers earlier in executive summary drafting
Framing percentage as evidence of governance adequacy
Implicit suggestion that no escalation was required due to deadline pressure
Stakeholder-facing wording softened internal cautionary language
Increased tolerance for recommendation-style phrasing under time constraints
uncertainty_notes: Definition of "AI-assisted" may vary across telemetry sources
Percentage metric does not indicate quality, risk level, or governance maturity
Telemetry capture may omit informal or undocumented AI usage
Stakeholder interpretation of percentage may differ from internal governance intent
Time pressure likely increased influence on tone and wording decisions
Escalation thresholds remain unquantified and were not re-evaluated under compressed timeline
Peer review limitations may have reduced detection of interpretive drift
Scenario does not simulate regulatory review or external audit conditions
escalation_triggers: Introduction of recommendation or threshold language without formal mandate
Persistent telemetry inconsistency exceeding defined tolerance
Stakeholder request to publish percentage as risk or adequacy indicator
Removal of uncertainty qualifiers from public-facing draft
Ambiguity regarding classification definition of AI-assisted content
Escalation requested by governance participant due to interpretive disagreement
Deadline-driven pressure to bypass formal review checkpoints
stop_or_reset_events: heightened monitoring required to maintain posture under deadline pressure

tensions: Speed of reporting vs thorough governance review
Transparency of uncertainty vs stakeholder demand for clarity
Telemetry-driven reporting vs qualitative governance judgment
affected_parties: End users affected by decisions informed by the metric
Senior leadership relying on rapid metric interpretation
potential_harms: Misinterpretation of percentage as quality or safety indicator
Erosion of uncertainty transparency in governance reporting
Scope creep into recommendation-making without mandate
Incorrect escalation decisions due to ambiguous thresholds
Increased likelihood of publishing metrics without fully reconciled telemetry
Reduced opportunity to detect wording that implies endorsement or adequacy
tradeoffs_noted: Deadline adherence vs full telemetry reconciliation
Rapid response vs deliberate escalation review
